div.p: I think it may interest you to know the fate of my book Dubliners which you reviewed so favourably. The publisher Mr Grant Richards sends me a statement of sales by which I see that 379 copies have been sold in the United Kingdom to date. I receive no royalty and was, in fact, obliged to buy and pay for 120 copies. This is the epilogue of what you called in your article a curious history.
I have appointed Mr Pinker my literary agent and have also given him the disposal of the dramatic rights of my play. Mr Grant Richards has not yet decided whether he will publish or not my novel .
I have not heard from you for some time and hope you are not ill again.

div.note: For JJ’s use of this wartime mailing address, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.

Pound had published a penetrating and positive review of Dubliners in The Egoist, vol. 1, no. 14 (15 July 1914): 267, under the title “‘Dubliners’ and Mr. James Joyce.” He stated there that JJ “writes a clear hard prose” and presents things “with such clarity of outline that he might be dealing with locomotives or with builders’ specifications.” JJ’s prose, Pound thought, had the “definiteness” of Flaubert and reflected an “international standard” rather than “the promotion of Irish peasant industries.” JJ’s “more rigorous selection of the presented detail marks him,” Pound added, “as belonging to my own generation” (267). A quotation from this review was printed in a two-page leaflet of press extracts issued in penetrating connection with the publication of Dubliners.

Grant Richards sent JJ an account of the sales of the English edition of Dubliners on 29 April 1915. The statement indicated that of the 1,250 copies printed, 117 had been given away free for review or promotion, and that 499 had been sold. These 499 copies were to be treated as 461 according to the royalty agreement by which thirteen copies counted as twelve. Of these 461 copies, JJ himself had purchased 120. Richards’ statement noted that “No royalty is payable till after 500 copies are sold” (Scholes, “Grant Richards to James Joyce,” 157-58). JJ apparently arrived at 379 as the number of copies sold by subtracting the 120 he had bought from the total of 499 sold, ignoring the thirteen-as-twelve arrangement. On 13 May 1915, Richards replied to JJ’s characterization of sales as “disastrous” by reminding him that he was a “new writer,” that collections of stories were “always handicapped,” and that there was a war on (Scholes, 158).

In The Egoist, vol. 1, no. 2 (15 January 1914): 26-27, Pound had published JJ’s grim account of the two publishers, Grant Richards in London and Maunsel & Co. in Dublin, that had contracted to publish Dubliners but later refused to do so without substantial changes to the collection or financial undertakings by JJ. The account, titled “A Curious History,” incorporated letters from JJ and was issued in May 1917 as a promotional broadside by B.W. Huebsch, the American publisher of Dubliners.
For the role of JJ’s agent, J.B. Pinker, in arrangements for Exiles and A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.

Grant Richards wrote to JJ on 18 May 1915, declining to exercise his option to publish A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and citing the war and “the general depression” as reasons. Richards added that the novel “demands a public of intelligent readers. There are such readers but they are … peculiarly difficult to get at now” (Scholes, 158-59). B.W. Huebsch of New York published A Portrait in December 1916, and the novel was first published as a book in England in February 1917 by the Egoist Ltd. of London.
Pound wrote to JJ ca. June 1915, stating that he felt it was “entirely vain and useless to write to you, at least until we know that the Italians have rescued Trieste” (Pound/Joyce 34).
